thought.text: The backend auth fails due to DNS. Let me verify the startup log and whether auth ever worked, and examine the frontend's title / sample data.

reasoning_content:
Let me get the public info endpoint content, and check the frontend HTML title. Also, let me test the full flow: does the sample data exist? Let me check if the VITE_AUTH_BYPASS is false which means the app requires Keycloak login and the backend auth needs Keycloak.

The core question: is the installation operational? The backend boots, serves API, DB is migrated, frontend serves. But the auth flow through backend fails because backend can't resolve `auth.localhost`. This is a DNS misconfiguration in the environment.

Let me determine whether this is an installation defect or an environment limitation. In the guide, HTTP mode uses `auth.localhost:3000` issuer. Browsers resolve `*.localhost` to 127.0.0.1 (per RFC 6761, modern browsers do this). So the intended access point is a browser on the same machine — but the backend running as a native process must resolve auth.localhost too. On a normal Linux dev machine, `auth.localhost` typically does NOT resolve via glibc (only newer systemd-resolved and some distros handle it). Actually, on most Linux systems `*.localhost` resolves to 127.0.0.1? Let me think. Historically, glibc doesn't resolve `foo.localhost`. systemd-resolved does resolve `*.localhost` to 127.0.0.1 (since v247 or so). Node also added special-casing. So on many dev machines it works.

Here the container lacks /etc/hosts entries for auth.localhost and DNS returns nothing. So the backend fails auth. Is this installation's fault? The installation summary says it started the backend and frontend and accessed via localhost:3000. The auth component is broken in this environment. Is this a genuine failure of the installation? The guide says "Open http://localhost:3000" and Keycloak at http://auth.localhost:3000. The user accesses the app through a browser (on the host?), but validation here is in the container. The frontend requires OIDC login (VITE_AUTH_BYPASS=false), and the backend rejects all protected API calls because JWKS fetch fails.

This is a significant operational problem: authenticated functionality is unavailable. The question is whether it's due to installation incompleteness or environment limitation. The install summary didn't mention adding `auth.localhost` to /etc/hosts. But also, the install used `localhost` as the host for accessing. Hmm.

Wait — actually let me re-examine. Is it possible that the backend's issue is intermittent? The JWKS refresh happens every 10s, logging "starting new connection" but no success. Let me check the backend log for whether initial JWKS ever succeeded. Let me grep.

Also, let me check `/etc/hosts` again — perhaps the installer intended to use a different issuer. But the running process env clearly shows APP_AUTH__ISSUER_URL=http://auth.localhost:3000/realms/green-ecolution.

Let me check whether the auth.localhost resolution could work through a proxy env var, or whether the app's own docker network handles it. In docker mode, the backend container would have extra_hosts or the compose network aliases. But here the backend runs natively (run-dev-ish).

Actually, wait. In the normal `just run-dev`, both backend and frontend run natively, and the browser accesses via Traefik. The backend needs to reach Keycloak at auth.localhost:3000. On a typical dev workstation with systemd-resolved, `*.localhost` resolves to 127.0.0.1. In this Docker-in-Docker container, it doesn't. So it's an environment limitation, but the outcome for the user is that auth doesn't work.

Hmm, this is the crux. Let me check whether maybe there's a compose-based approach that would work, or whether the intended access is via browser with the backend resolving. Let me check if the app might be considered "operational" for the guide's purposes.

The guide's quick start: `just infra-up; just migrate-up; just run-dev; open localhost:3000`. The install summary did exactly this (manually). The resulting environment has auth broken due to DNS. 

Let me verify whether perhaps the backend can resolve auth.localhost via a different mechanism (e.g., maybe it uses the Host header loop). No, log clearly shows connection attempts failing.

Let me double check by looking at full backend startup log to see if initial JWKS refresh failed, and check if there were any successful auth requests.

action.command: cd /workspace && echo "=== jwks / keycloak lines in backend log ==="; grep -a -i "jwks\|keycloak\|identity provider\|loaded JWKS\|refresh" /tmp/backend.log | sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' | head -20; echo "=== startup head ==="; sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/backend.log | head -25
